caption: "permanent daylight savings time" — 50,000+ searches this week, up 1,000%. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the clock change.

Why: the House passed the Sunshine Protection Act on July 14, 308 to 117, for permanent daylight time. The Senate committee hasn't voted. The Senate has 14 session days left and returns November 9, after clocks fall back November 1.

What most people don't know: America tried permanent daylight time in 1974 and quit within a year after children died walking to school in the dark; support fell from 79% to 42%. Hawaii and most of Arizona never change. Nineteen states are ready to switch.
Very simply put: House yes, 19 states ready, clocks still fall back.

slides.headline: The House voted to end clock changes. The clocks *fall back* anyway.

slides.headline: The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House *308 to 117*.
slides.sub: July 14, 2026. The Senate passed the same idea by unanimous consent in 2022; that time the House never voted.
slides.image: A grand domed legislative building at golden hour under a clear sky, dome in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain stone steps, photorealistic, no people, no flags, no text

slides.headline: The Senate has *14 session days* before it leaves.
slides.sub: 12 in September, 2 in October. It adjourns October 2 and returns November 9. Clocks fall back November 1.
slides.image: An hourglass with sand running low on a dark wooden table, hourglass in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain dark wood, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: Trump: 'Saving Daylight' gives a *longer, brighter day*.
slides.sub: His stated position. Sleep doctors want the opposite: permanent standard time, which matches the body clock better.
slides.image: Low golden evening sun over a quiet suburban street with long shadows, sky in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain asphalt, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: The US already tried it in *1974*. It lasted a year.
slides.sub: Year-round daylight time began January 6, 1974, to save fuel in the oil embargo.
slides.image: A 1970s gas station forecourt at dusk with vintage pumps, pumps in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain concrete, photorealistic, no people, no logos, no text

slides.headline: Support fell from *79% to 42%* in three months.
slides.sub: After morning crashes killed schoolchildren walking in the dark, including eight in Florida. Congress ended it in 1975.
slides.image: An empty school bus stop sign on a dark street before dawn with one streetlight, sign in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wet road, photorealistic, no people, no readable text

slides.headline: *19 states* have laws ready to switch.
slides.sub: Texas, Florida, Georgia, Washington, Oregon and Colorado among them. They need Congress to say yes.
slides.image: A paper map of the United States with several states shaded in yellow, map in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wooden table, photorealistic, no readable text

slides.headline: Hawaii and most of *Arizona* never change.
slides.sub: The Navajo Nation inside Arizona does. Five US territories stay on standard time too.
slides.image: Red desert rock formations under a bright midday sky, rocks in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain sand, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: It started in *1918*, and the dates keep moving.
slides.sub: Standard Time Act, March 19, 1918. National rules came in 1966; a 2005 law added four to five weeks.
